findings.measured: Almost no content above 16 kHz; check whether an MP3/AAC or low-passed file was used as a source.

steps.text: Check the session for MP3 or AAC files, such as samples or imported references.
Look for a low-pass filter on the master or a bus cutting everything above 16 kHz.

findings.measured: Contrast is 1.7 LU; typical for Trap / hip-hop is 2.5 to 7 LU.

steps.text: Press A for automation mode and draw volume so verses sit 2–3 dB below choruses.

other_options.text: Ease the mix-bus compressor: raise the threshold or slow the attack so transients get through.

notes.headline: This mix is technically clean and ready for mastering — the only two notes are informational: no content above 16 kHz, and less loud/quiet contrast than typical trap.
notes.summary: Nothing here is broken. Levels, headroom and stereo behaviour all check out: -17.11 LUFS integrated with a true peak of -4.14 dBTP leaves mastering plenty of room, and the low end holds together in mono. Two things are worth a look before you hand it off. There's almost nothing above 16 kHz, which usually means an MP3/AAC source or a low-pass somewhere, and your loudness range is 1.68 LU where trap/hip-hop usually sits between 2.5 and 7 LU — that's a choice, but worth knowing you've made it.

priorities.title: Track down the missing top above 16 kHz
priorities.why: Almost no content above 16 kHz normally points at a lossy source file or a low-pass left on a bus. Mastering can't put back what isn't there, so it's worth finding now rather than after the fact.

priorities.title: Decide whether you want more contrast
priorities.why: At 1.68 LU the mix stays at one level throughout, against 2.5 to 7 LU typical for trap/hip-hop. If the song is meant to lift into the hook, mastering compression will flatten it further, so build the difference in the mix.

listen_for: Play the mix against a track you know has real top end — cymbals and hats above 16 kHz — on headphones, and see whether yours sounds closed off or just dark by design.
Solo any imported samples and check whether they sound dull or swishy on their own, which would point at an MP3/AAC source.
Listen to the transition from verse into the hook and ask whether the hook actually arrives, or whether everything sits at one level.
Check the low end in mono on a single speaker or phone — it measured tight, confirm it still is after any changes.
strengths: True peak at -4.14 dBTP and -17.11 LUFS integrated: exactly the headroom a mastering engineer wants.
Low-end correlation of 0.969 and only 0.91 dB mono loss — your bass stays solid on mono playback.
Left/right balance is -0.39 dB, essentially centred.

judge.priority_order: Both findings are info severity; the notes put F1 (missing high-frequency content, unfixable in mastering) before F2 (loudness range choice), which is a reasonable ranking of audible consequence.
judge.explains_impact: F1 explains 'mastering can't put back what isn't there' and F2 explains the mix 'stays at one level throughout' with hook-flattening consequences.
judge.groups_causes: F1 and F2 are unrelated causes (source file vs. dynamics) and are correctly kept as separate priorities rather than merged.
judge.specific: Notes cite exact LUFS (-17.11), true peak (-4.14 dBTP), correlation (0.969), mono loss (0.91 dB), LU range (1.68 vs 2.5-7) and genre (trap/hip-hop).
judge.stage_appropriate: Notes correctly frame headroom as good for mastering and don't fault loudness, consistent with the mix stage.
judge.faithful: All numbers and claims match the report; the LU-range difference is framed as 'a choice' rather than an error, consistent with the report's neutral info severity.
judge.concise: Given two findings plus strengths, the notes stay focused on report content without hype or filler, though the summary slightly restates the headline.
